tagline: From valley farmland to Cascade forest, beside an old freight route.
intro: The Over the Rivers & Through the Woods Scenic Byway climbs from Willamette Valley farmland into the Cascades, winding beside streams and through dense forest. Oregon’s transportation department identifies this 66-mile scenic byway as a journey through five Western Oregon ecosystems, with access to rivers, reservoirs and trails. It gives a minimum driving time of two to three hours.

Much of the drive parallels the Santiam Wagon Road, built to take settlers east to central Oregon pastures and gold mines in eastern Oregon and Idaho. The toll road carried livestock and goods east and wool back to Willamette Valley mills. Tolls ended in 1915, and the road passed to the state in 1925 for highway use. U.S. 20 was later built across much of the wagon road’s route.

From Interstate 5, head east through Brownsville and Crawfordsville, then bend north from Holley to Sweet Home. U.S. 20 continues past Foster Reservoir and follows the South Santiam River through Cascadia. Near Mountain House, the road leaves the river and gains more than 2,500 feet in seven miles toward 4,241-foot Tombstone Pass. Near the eastern end, Hackleman Old Growth Trail passes trees more than 500 years old before the byway reaches the Route 20/126 junction.

moments.title: Brownsville
moments.text: Brownsville became a film location in June and July 1985, when Rob Reiner shot Stand by Me in and near the community. About 100 local residents appeared as extras. The film reached theaters in August 1986. The first Stand by Me Day followed in 2007, and the celebration continues annually, with 2020 omitted during the pandemic. Local film expert Linda McCormick recalled choosing July 23 to avoid conflicts with regional events and the start of school. The town’s Main Street also retains historic buildings preserved to look much as they did a century ago.

moments.title: Crawfordsville Bridge
moments.text: Crawfordsville’s covered bridge still crosses the Calapooia River beside Oregon Route 228, but highway traffic bypassed it in 1963. Built in 1932, the 105-foot Howe truss span now serves pedestrians under the care of Linn County Parks & Recreation. A small park next to the bridge provides a picnic table and fire pit. The crossing also appeared in the 1976 television movie The Flood.
moments.notice: The covered span crosses the Calapooia beside the highway.

moments.title: Cascadia
moments.text: Old wagon ruts remain visible near the meeting of Soda Creek and the South Santiam River at Cascadia County Park. Cascadia began as a stage stop on the Santiam Wagon Road before becoming a summer resort. In 1896, George Geisendorfer opened a resort promoting what he called the “curative powers” of the mineral spring water. The resort once included tennis courts, a croquet course and a bowling alley. Its hotel later burned, and Oregon acquired the property in 1940. The former state park transferred to Linn County in September 2022; trails lead along Soda Creek and down to the river.
moments.notice: Wagon ruts are visible near the confluence of Soda Creek and the South Santiam River.
